summaries.example: Think about a particular dog named Pepper. Pepper is a dog, and many philosophers would say Pepper could not have been a different kind of thing, such as a bicycle. That makes being a dog an essential property for Pepper. Pepper’s favorite toy is different: Pepper could have liked another toy, so that is an accidental property.
summaries.summary:
The entry explains a difference between two kinds of properties. An essential property is a feature a thing must have. An accidental property is a feature it has now but could have lacked. For example, philosophers often say that being human is essential to a particular human, while liking dogs is accidental. They also discuss possible worlds, which are ways the world might have been, to help explain “must” and “could.”

The simple account has puzzles. A dog named Emma might not have existed, and in a possible world where Emma does not exist, she is not a dog. This can make “being a dog” seem accidental, even though it seems right to say Emma is essentially a dog if she exists. Existence therefore needs special care in the discussion.

Philosophers have proposed other approaches. Some connect essence with what defines a thing. Others connect it with the deepest explanations of a thing’s features. The entry also describes kinds of essentialism, including claims about an object’s kind, its origin, or properties that uniquely identify it. Finally, it explains how essential properties can be used in arguments about whether two things are really the same.
key_ideas: An essential property is something a thing must have; an accidental property is something it happens to have.
Philosophers often use ideas about necessity and possibility to explain the difference.
Some philosophers think an object’s kind or its origin is essential to it.
There is disagreement about exactly how to define “essential.”
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us ask what makes something the thing it is. It also shows why words such as “must,” “could,” and “same” need careful thought. These ideas are used when philosophers discuss people, animals, natural kinds such as water, and objects made from the same material. The topic also teaches an important lesson: a simple definition can be useful but may create new puzzles.

important_terms.definition: A feature or way of being that something has, such as being a dog, being large, or liking a toy.
A property that something could not be without, according to a philosophical view.
A property that something has but could have lacked.
A way things might have been, used by philosophers to think about possibilities.
A claim that some things have at least some essential properties.

questions_to_think_about: Could a particular dog have been a cat? Why or why not?
Is your favorite color essential to you, or could it have been different?
Can two things share the same place but still have different essential properties?

summaries.example: Imagine a statue named Goliath made from a lump of wax called Lump1. They occupy exactly the same place and have the same weight. If the wax melts and later cools into a mountain-like shape, one might say Goliath no longer exists while Lump1 still does. An essentialist argument says that Goliath is essentially human-shaped, whereas Lump1 is not. By Leibniz’s Law—the principle that identical things share all their properties—Goliath and Lump1 therefore cannot be identical. Philosophers disagree about whether this argument is valid, whether it assumes what it is trying to prove, or whether one of its premises is false.
summaries.summary:
The entry examines the distinction between essential and accidental properties. On the basic modal characterization, a property P is essential to an object o if o must have P; P is accidental if o has P but could lack it. Philosophers often express this using possible worlds. “Must” indicates necessity, while “could” indicates possibility. The relevant modality is generally metaphysical possibility, not merely epistemic possibility, which concerns what an agent does not know to be false.

The modal account faces a problem involving existence. A particular dog, Emma, might not have existed. In a possible world where Emma does not exist, she is not a dog, which seems to make being a dog accidental. Yet it is intuitive that Emma is essentially a dog, at least if she exists. An existence-conditioned version tries to solve this, but it can make existence essential to every object and thereby affect substantive claims about whether only God has existence essentially. The entry sets aside these technical details while noting that existence may require special treatment.

Other accounts challenge the idea that every necessary property is essential. Kit Fine argues that essence concerns an object’s nature or definition: facts such as the existence of infinitely many prime numbers may be necessary without being part of what Socrates is. Alternatives refine the modal approach by distinguishing kinds of objects, using local possibility, nonstandard counterfactuals, sparse properties, or intrinsic properties. An explanatory approach identifies essence with an object’s deepest explanatory features, though this may make essence relative to explanatory aims.

key_ideas: The standard modal account treats an essential property as necessary for an object and an accidental property as one the object could lack.
Existence creates a problem: if an object might not have existed, it may not have had properties that require existence, such as being a dog.
A definition-based account links essence to what belongs to an object’s nature, but it faces the question of what it means to define an object.
An explanatory account identifies essential properties with the deepest properties that explain an object’s other features, but explanation may depend partly on explanatory interests.
Essentialism has several forms, including minimal, maximal, origin, sortal, and natural-kind essentialism.
Essentialist claims can support arguments about nonidentity, although philosophers dispute some such arguments.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction matters because it concerns identity, change, and the structure of reality. It asks whether an object can survive changes in its features, origin, kind, or material. It also separates metaphysical claims from claims about language: an object’s name or description may vary even when the object’s essential properties do not. Finally, essentialist claims often appear in arguments about nonidentity, including arguments involving minds and bodies or statues and their material. Studying the disputes reveals how philosophical arguments can depend on subtle assumptions about necessity, definitions, explanation, and identity.

important_terms.definition: A property an object has in every metaphysically possible situation, or, in a qualified version, whenever that object exists.
A property an object actually has but could lack while continuing to exist.
A way of analyzing a claim using necessity and possibility rather than only what is actual.
Possibility concerning how reality could be, distinguished from merely not knowing that something is false.
The view that at least some objects have at least some essential properties.
The view that an object could not have originated in a radically different way from its actual origin.
The view that an object could not have been a radically different kind of thing from the kind it actually is.
The principle that identical objects must share all their properties; it can be used to argue that two apparently different things are not identical.

questions_to_think_about: Does being a dog seem essential to a particular dog even if that dog could have failed to exist? How should a theory explain this?
Is a property essential because it is necessary, because it belongs to a definition, or because it explains other properties?
How is metaphysical possibility different from merely not knowing whether something is true?
Does the statue-and-wax case show that two objects can occupy exactly the same place?
Can a necessary truth about a kind, such as water being H2O, show that every particular sample has that property essentially?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya owns a red skateboard and is very good at drawing. Could Maya have owned a blue skateboard instead? Probably yes, so those features look accidental. Could Maya have been a skateboard instead of a person? Many essentialists would say no: being human is part of what Maya is. They might also ask whether Maya could have come from completely different biological origins. Some would say her actual origin is essential too. Other philosophers think the word “essential” should be connected less to every necessary fact and more closely to what makes Maya the kind of thing she is.
summaries.summary:
This entry explores how philosophers separate essential properties from accidental ones. An essential property is one a thing must have; an accidental property is one it has in fact but could have lacked. The standard approach is modal: it explains the difference through necessity and possibility. Philosophers sometimes describe possible worlds as complete ways reality might have been. Metaphysical possibility is not simply a person’s uncertainty. Something may be unknown without being genuinely possible, and something may be possible even though we already know it is not actual.

The standard approach creates a puzzle about existence. A dog named Emma might never have existed. In a possible world where Emma does not exist, she is not a dog. Yet many people think Emma is essentially a dog, at least when considering worlds in which she exists. An existence-conditioned version tries to handle this, but it risks making existence essential to every object. The entry treats this as a reason to be cautious rather than as a final solution.

A second debate concerns necessary properties that do not seem to describe what a thing is. For example, Socrates necessarily has some properties simply because certain mathematical facts are necessary. Kit Fine argues that such facts need not belong to Socrates’s essence. He connects essence with an object’s definition or nature, but this raises a difficult question: objects such as numbers may seem definable, while particular people do not have definitions in the same obvious way. Other philosophers revise the modal account using ideas such as intrinsic properties, fundamental properties, or special kinds of possible worlds.

The entry also compares versions of essentialism. Minimal essentialism allows only very weak essential properties;
key_ideas: The usual account says that essential properties are necessary, while accidental properties are changeable possibilities.
Philosophers distinguish metaphysical possibility from simply not knowing whether something is true.
A basic account has trouble with objects that could have failed to exist, because properties such as being a dog may require existence.
Some philosophers connect essence with an object’s definition or nature instead of with every property it has necessarily.
Essentialism comes in stronger and weaker forms, and philosophers disagree about which forms deserve the name.
Claims about essence can be used to argue that two things are not identical, even when they look alike or share a location.
summaries.why_it_matters: Essential and accidental properties give us a vocabulary for thinking about change and identity. They help explain why changing a color or hobby may leave something the same, while changing its kind or origin might not. The distinction also appears in debates about natural kinds, such as whether water must be H2O, and in arguments about whether two objects are really one thing. Because the topic connects everyday ideas with difficult questions about possibility, it is a useful introduction to metaphysics.

important_terms.definition: A feature something has, such as being human, being red, or being good at drawing.
A feature that a thing must have and could not lack, according to a theory of essence.
A feature a thing has but could have lacked while remaining that thing.
A way things might have been. Philosophers use possible worlds to discuss what could or could not happen.
A property or claim about what must be the case or could be the case.
The view that some things have properties they could not lack.
The idea that a thing could not have begun from a completely different origin.
The idea that a thing could not have been a completely different kind of thing.

questions_to_think_about: Could your name be different while you remained the same person? Would that make your name accidental?
Why might being human seem more essential than having a certain hairstyle?
Should a fact that is necessary for everything, such as a mathematical fact, count as part of every object’s essence?
What problem appears when we compare an object with a possible world in which it never exists?
Can two objects share the same material and place but still have different essential properties?
